articles.title: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices
authors: Cardiology/CV Surgery Section, Pulmonary Vascular Disease and Cardiovascular Network.

abstract.text: Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.

articles.title: Right ventricular failure across load and myocardial phenotypes: anatomy, plasticity and therapeutic implications
articles.journal: European heart journal. Imaging methods and practice
articles.journal_abbrev: Eur Heart J Imaging Methods Pract
articles.ta: Eur Heart J Imaging Methods Pract

abstract.text: The right ventricle (RV) is a load-dependent chamber whose performance reflects myocardial reserve, loading conditions, and ventricular interdependence. Volume overload, pressure overload, and intrinsic myocardial dysfunction produce distinct, often overlapping remodelling trajectories and therapeutic targets. This review integrated contemporary imaging and prognostic evidence into a mechanism-to-decision framework. Its clinical contribution is to explain how deformation and chamber geometry should be interpreted with regurgitant burden and forward flow in volume overload, vascular load and coupling in pressure overload, and regional motion and tissue injury in intrinsic disease. Echocardiography combines these measurements with valve assessment, pulmonary outflow Doppler, left-heart filling phenotype and systemic venous congestion. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance, computed tomography, right heart catheterization and stress testing resolve selected anatomical or physiological uncertainty. Automated measurements can support serial phenotyping but require image and contour review. Reverse remodelling describes favourable structural change; meaningful recovery additionally requires preserved or restored effective forward performance and improvement in clinical or venous consequences after treatment of the causal load, lesion or myocardial substrate. This framework helps recognize discordant findings, select further assessment and judge treatment response without equating a single load-dependent index with myocardial recovery.

articles.title: Effect of lung transplantation on biventricular function in pulmonary arterial hypertension: A systematic review

abstract.text: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) leads to progressive right ventricular (RV) failure and secondary left ventricular (LV) dysfunction due to chronic pressure overload and ventricular interdependence. Lung transplantation (LTx) is an established treatment for end-stage PAH, yet patterns of biventricular recovery and the role of veno-arterial perioperative extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) remain incompletely defined. A PubMed search identified studies published from 1990 to 2025 using MeSH terms related to lung transplantation, ventricular function, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, and ECMO. Prospective studies, retrospective analyses, and case series evaluating post-transplant cardiac function in PAH were included. A total of 13 studies were included. Across studies, LTx resulted in rapid and substantial RV reverse remodeling, with improvements in RV size, mass, systolic function, tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary pressures. This reduction in RV afterload was accompanied by progressive improvement of RV output. In contrast, LV recovery was more variable, possibly due to chronic underfilling and LV remodeling. Cardiac MRI and echocardiography demonstrated progressive biventricular structural and functional adaptation over time. Perioperative VA-ECMO may provide hemodynamic support during this transition by unloading the RV and maintaining perfusion while ventricular loading conditions rapidly change. Lung transplantation for PAH initiates transition from chronic RV pressure overload and LV underfilling to improved pulmonary vascular conditions and subsequent biventricular recovery. Further longitudinal studies are needed to identify predictors of maladaptive LV responses and determine which patients may benefit from prolonged perioperative VA-ECMO support.

articles.title: Inhaled nitric oxide use facilitated VA-ECMO weaning during ECPELLA support in a patient with a precapillary pulmonary vascular phenotype: a case report

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Combined support with veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) and a micro-axial flow pump (mAFP), termed ECPELLA, provides systemic circulatory support with left ventricular (LV) unloading in refractory cardiogenic shock. VA-ECMO weaning may nevertheless be difficult when pulmonary vascular afterload is increased despite adequate LV unloading. Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) selectively reduces pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), but its role in this setting remains unclear.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: An 83-year-old woman with non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome underwent percutaneous coronary intervention. Persistent circulatory collapse required mAFP support followed by VA-ECMO. Despite adequate LV unloading, pulmonary artery catheterization showed low pulmonary artery catheter-derived cardiac output (PAC-CO), low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and high calculated PVR, suggesting increased pulmonary vascular afterload rather than residual LV congestion. VA-ECMO flow reduction caused hypotension. After administration of iNO at 40 ppm, PAC-CO increased from 1.2 to 1.5 L/min and calculated PVR decreased from 11.7 to 8.0 Wood units while mechanical circulatory support settings and ventilator settings remained unchanged. VA-ECMO was removed on Day 2 and the mAFP on Day 3. The patient nevertheless died on Day 4 from complications of severe lower-limb ischaemia.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: A relative increase in PVR may hinder VA-ECMO weaning during ECPELLA support. iNO may facilitate device weaning in selected patients; however, a temporal association in a single case does not establish causality, clinical recovery, or a survival benefit.

articles.title: Acute right ventricular response to transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement
articles.journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Changes in right ventricular (RV) function are frequent after transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR), yet their mechanisms and prognostic implications remain incompletely defined.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: We sought to characterise acute RV functional changes following TTVR and evaluate their prognostic impact.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This multicentre study included consecutive patients treated with TTVR between 2019 and 2025 with complete imaging data. RV function was assessed by echocardiography at baseline, intraprocedurally, and before discharge. RV end-systolic elastance (Ees), effective arterial elastance (Ea), and RV-pulmonary artery coupling (Ees/Ea) were derived from non-invasive single-beat pressure-volume loop analysis. Changes over time were assessed using paired tests, and associations with mortality were investigated using Cox regression analysis with Firth's penalised likelihood.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Sixty-seven patients (median age 78 years; 72% female; EVOQUE n=49; LuX-Valve Plus n=18) were included. At discharge, both cohorts showed declines in absolute RV free-wall longitudinal strain (aRV-FWLS; -10.4%; p<0.001 for EVOQUE; -10.4%; p=0.001 for LuX-Valve Plus) and fractional area change (FAC; -18.0%; p<0.001 for EVOQUE; -13.5%; p=0.005 for LuX-Valve Plus). Overall, 58% of patients met the criteria for severe RV dysfunction after TTVR. Over a median follow-up of 19 months, 15 patients died. Device type, acute RV functional changes, Ees, and Ees/Ea were not associated with mortality (allp>0.05). In contrast, computed tomography-derived RV coupling (hazard ratio [HR] 0.02, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.01-0.89) and the coexistence of baseline longitudinal (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion <17 mm and/or aRV-FWLS <23%) and circumferential (RV-FAC ≤35%) RV dysfunction (HR 3.93, 95% CI: 1.10-14.47) were associated with mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: TTVR is associated with an acute decline in RV systolic function. Although common, early postprocedural RV dysfunction was not associated with midterm mortality.

articles.conclusion: TTVR is associated with an acute decline in RV systolic function. Although common, early postprocedural RV dysfunction was not associated with midterm mortality.

articles.title: Prevalence of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Associated with Congenital Heart Disease Following Defect Correction: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
articles.journal: European heart journal. Quality of care & clinical outcomes
articles.journal_abbrev: Eur Heart J Qual Care Clin Outcomes
articles.ta: Eur Heart J Qual Care Clin Outcomes

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Understanding the disease burden of repaired pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with congenital heart disease (PAH-CHD) is essential for guiding healthcare strategies, yet data are lacking in this area.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To estimate the prevalence of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) following defect correction in patients with congenital heart disease (CHD).

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed using PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases.

abstract.label: STUDY SELECTION
abstract.text: Longitudinal cohort published between 1970-2023 involving CHD patients who underwent defect correction and were subsequently diagnosed with PAH were reviewed. Eligible studies reporting the prevalence of repaired PAH-CHD at least 3 months post-repair was included. Study selection was conducted independently by two reviewers. The primary outcome was the prevalence of PAH in patients following CHD defect correction.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Across 58 studies (7,036 participants), the random-effects pooled prevalence of reported post-repair PAH/PH was 10.8% (95% CI 7.3-15.0, I2 = 95.6%; prediction interval 0-50.1%). Prevalence was 9.0% (95% CI 3.3-17) in studies using right heart catheterisation, 19.3% (CI 10.6-29.7) in studies using echocardiography and 16.1% (CI 8.6- 25.1%) in studies using both modalities (p=0.19). Prevalence was highest in the adult-only cohort (18.5%, 95%CI 11.8-26.2) and lower in paediatric only (7.6%, 95%CI 3-13.5) and mixed-age cohorts (7.5%,95%CI1.7-16.3), p=0.039. Preoperative pulmonary hypertension (PH) was the strongest predictor of post-repair PAH and remained predictive on adjusted meta-regression (p<0.01).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: PAH following defect repair remains a significant clinical dilemma requiring standardised diagnostic criteria and robust risk stratification tools to guide management.

articles.conclusion: PAH following defect repair remains a significant clinical dilemma requiring standardised diagnostic criteria and robust risk stratification tools to guide management.

articles.title: Thermodynamic Response During Invasive Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Core temperature is continuously measured during invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (iCPET), but its physiologic and clinical significance remains poorly defined.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: The purpose of this study was to characterize exercise core temperature responses during iCPET and determine whether temperature-derived metrics are associated with cardiopulmonary reserve, abnormal physiologic phenotypes, and clinically relevant iCPET thresholds.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We studied 396 adults undergoing iCPET for unexplained exertional intolerance. Core temperature was measured using the thermistor of a pulmonary artery catheter. Temperature-derived metrics included peak exercise temperature, increase in temperature from baseline to peak exercise, and increase in temperature indexed to peak workload. Associations with hemodynamic and gas-exchange variables were assessed using age- and sex-adjusted models. Area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC) analyses evaluated discrimination for normal vs abnormal iCPET findings and selected physiologic thresholds.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Participants were 50.6 ± 16.0 years old, and 66% were female. Core temperature increased during exercise from 37.0 °C ± 0.34 °C at baseline to 37.5 °C ± 0.51 °C at peak exercise, with a mean increase of 0.40 °C ± 0.37 °C. Temperature-derived metrics were directly associated with peak cardiac index and percent-predicted peak oxygen uptake and inversely associated with pulmonary artery occlusion pressure/cardiac output slope and minute ventilation/carbon dioxide production slope. Temperature responses were blunted in heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, chronotropic incompetence, and impaired peripheral oxygen extraction. For identifying a normal test, age- and sex-adjusted AUCs were 0.70 for peak exercise temperature, 0.74 for increase in temperature, and 0.68 for workload-indexed temperature increase.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Exercise core temperature responses during iCPET reflect hemodynamic augmentation and aerobic performance and may provide a simple adjunctive physiologic marker for clinically relevant exercise abnormalities.

articles.conclusion: Exercise core temperature responses during iCPET reflect hemodynamic augmentation and aerobic performance and may provide a simple adjunctive physiologic marker for clinically relevant exercise abnormalities.

articles.title: Prognostic Value of Longitudinal Echo-Dynamic Assessment in Patients with Cardiogenic Shock A multi-center prospective study
articles.journal: European heart journal. Acute cardiovascular care
articles.journal_abbrev: Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care
articles.ta: Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: In cardiogenic shock (CS), early hemodynamic changes are associated with in-hospital outcomes, but evidence on non-invasive assessment is limited. We evaluated the prognostic value of a comprehensive non-invasive hemodynamic assessment by echocardiography ("echo-dynamics") at presentation and 48 hours in CS.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Consecutive CS patients at four Cardiac Intensive Care Units were prospectively enrolled. Echo-dynamics were obtained at baseline and 48 hours, including stroke volume index (SVi), cardiac index (CI), cardiac power output (CPO), estimated left atrial pressure (E/e'), systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (eSPAP) and right atrial pressure. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital mortality, left ventricular assist device implantation or heart transplantation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 457 patients (37.9% acute myocardial infarction-CS, 42.9% SCAI CS stage ≥C, 28% mean ejection fraction), the primary outcome occurred in 30.0%. Each echo-dynamic parameter was associated with the outcome at both time points after adjustment for age, sex, CS etiology and severity. Changes from baseline to 48 hours showed a stepwise risk increase across improving, worsening, or persistently abnormal trajectories (p-trend<0.01). In fully adjusted models, baseline CPO<0.6 W (adj-OR 2.05, 95%CI 1.29-3.26) and eSPAP ≥35 mmHg (adj-OR 2.45, 95%CI 1.44-4.15) were associated with outcomes; at 48 hours, CPO<0.6 W (adj-OR 2.70, 95%CI 1.57-4.66), increased E/e' (adj-OR 1.86, 95%CI 1.09-3.15) and eSPAP ≥35 mmHg (adj-OR 1.90, 95%CI 1.12-3.22) remained independently associated. Results were consistent when adjusting for SCAI stage.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In CS, longitudinal echo-dynamic assessment identifies distinct trajectories with prognostic implications. Persistently low cardiac power, and elevated filling and pulmonary pressures showed the strongest association with adverse outcomes.

articles.conclusion: In CS, longitudinal echo-dynamic assessment identifies distinct trajectories with prognostic implications. Persistently low cardiac power, and elevated filling and pulmonary pressures showed the strongest association with adverse outcomes.

articles.title: Longitudinal Cardiac Remodeling in High-Output Heart Failure From Intravascular Leiomyomatosis

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Intravascular leiomyomatosis can extend into nearby pelvic vasculature and to sites as distant as the heart and form arteriovenous malformations, leading to shunting and eventual high-output heart failure.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 45-year-old woman with biopsy-proven intravascular leiomyomatosis presented with biventricular dysfunction. Right heart catheterization demonstrated significant left-to-right shunting with high cardiac output. Serial echocardiography over 12 years showed the development of both left- and right-sided cardiac dysfunction. With treatment, left ventricular function recovered; however, right ventricular dilation and functional tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation established a self-sustaining cycle of right-sided failure.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Prior reports capture a single point in time; this 12-year echocardiographic course documents how shunt-mediated volume overload can progress to structural, self-perpetuating right heart failure independent of the original precipitant.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Shunt-mediated high-output heart failure can produce progressive cardiovascular deterioration. Early recognition and multidisciplinary care are essential to prevent irreversible structural remodeling.

articles.title: Atrial Flutter in Adolescence Due to Invasive Cardiac Lipoma: A Rare Presentation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Primary cardiac tumors are rare, with lipomas comprising ∼10% of benign cases. Although typically asymptomatic, invasive variants may infiltrate myocardium and generate significant arrhythmogenic substrate.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 14-year-old previously healthy male patient presented with atrial flutter and was found to have a large, infiltrative lipomatous mass involving the right atrium, right ventricle, and tricuspid valve. Biopsy and partial debulking confirmed invasive cardiac lipoma, but complete excision was precluded by extensive myocardial infiltration. Despite antiarrhythmic therapy, he developed recurrent atrial flutter and ventricular dysfunction. Electrophysiology study identified a cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter that was successfully ablated; however, a second tumor-associated circuit was not amenable to ablation because of anatomical barriers. Sinus rhythm was restored with cardioversion and amiodarone with subsequent recovery of ventricular function.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Invasive cardiac lipomas present unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, often requiring multimodal imaging, multidisciplinary management, aggressive rhythm control, and consideration of cardiac transplantation in select patients.

articles.title: Giant cell myocarditis mimicking cardiac amyloidosis with apical sparing pattern in echocardiography: a case report

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Giant cell myocarditis typically has a poor prognosis among the various types of myocarditis. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to save lives. Immunosuppressive therapy is used for giant cell myocarditis; however, evidence in patients on mechanical circulatory support is insufficient.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A woman in her 60 s with no history of heart disease or medication was admitted to our hospital because of congestive heart failure. Echocardiography revealed an apical sparing pattern suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. However, owing to the rapid deterioration of symptoms, an urgent right heart catheterization and myocardial biopsy were performed. Right heart catheterization revealed a cardiac index of 1.20 L/min/m2, and rapid myocardial histology indicated inflammatory cell infiltration. She was later diagnosed with giant cell myocarditis with cellular infiltration of irregular multinucleated giant cells in the myocardium. Her condition improved after starting mechanical circulatory support and sequential immunosuppressive therapy, and after successful rehabilitation, she was discharged as an outpatient on Day 183.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Early diagnosis and prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy are essential in giant cell myocarditis; however, specific findings are lacking. Early myocardial biopsy and prompt mechanical circulatory support initiation should be performed in patients with rapidly deteriorating heart failure presenting with amyloidosis-like echocardiographic findings and in cases where only troponin is elevated and creatine phosphokinase MB is not, considering the possibility of severe oedema. Combination immunosuppressive therapy under mechanical circulatory support is associated with a high infection risk, and starting with single-drug immunosuppressive therapy with careful haemodynamic monitoring is acceptable.

articles.title: Cardiac Output and Oxygen Delivery Responses to Sotatercept in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension

abstract.text: Sotatercept, a first-in-class activin signaling inhibitor, improves pulmonary vascular hemodynamics and clinical outcomes in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). However, despite reductions in mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), cardiac output (CO) does not generally increase, and some patients experience a decline in CO, a finding of unclear clinical significance. We sought to characterize the heterogeneity of CO responses to sotatercept in PAH and to determine whether incorporating oxygen delivery (DO2) provides additional insight into the physiological significance of these changes. We retrospectively analyzed PAH patients who underwent right heart catheterization before and during sotatercept therapy (median 7.3 months, IQR 4.8, 9.3). Hemodynamic, echocardiographic, hematologic, and clinical parameters were collected, including functional class, 6-min walk distance (6MWD) and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP). Patients were dichotomized by CO response (decreased vs. maintained), and DO2 was calculated at each catheterization. A total of 56 patients were included. While most demonstrated reductions in PVR and mPAP, 63% experienced decreased CO. Improvements in 6MWD and NT-proBNP were similar between groups, and hemoglobin increased comparably. However, among patients with decreased CO, 63% had a concomitant decline in DO2 accompanied by worsening 6MWD and a reduced NT-proBNP response. In this real-world cohort, over half of sotatercept-treated PAH patients experienced reduced CO despite overall hemodynamic and clinical improvement. Concomitant reductions in DO2 identify a subgroup with worse functional outcomes. These findings suggest that DO2 adds additional information beyond CO alone when assessing the physiological response to sotatercept.

articles.title: Imaging Biomarkers for Pulmonary Hypertension: AI-Based Vascular Analysis Through Non-Contrast Chest Computed Tomography Scans

abstract.text: Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) is a progressive, debilitating condition characterized by elevated pressures in the pulmonary vasculature. Accurate diagnosis and appropriate classification are essential for effective management of this disorder. This study evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)-based artery-vein phenotyping analysis (AVX) of non-contrast chest computed tomography (CT) scans as a means to improve diagnostic precision. A retrospective cohort study was conducted that enrolled patients who underwent non-contrast chest CT and right heart catheterization within a 6-month period. AVX provided segmentation and quantification of pulmonary arterial and venous trees, enabling an examination of vascular volume distribution. Radiological biomarkers were examined in the context of both PH classification and hemodynamic profiles. Significant differences in pulmonary vascular volumes were observed between three of the PH diagnostic groups (Group 1, Group 2, and Group 3, N = 163 patients). Patients stratified by hemodynamic profiles (pre-, isolated post-, and combined pre- and post-capillary) also showed distinct patterns of arterial and venous volumes. Several CT-derived vascular biomarkers were correlated with invasive hemodynamic measurements. Collectively, our findings suggest that the use of AI-based artery-vein quantification tools may provide complementary information for characterizing pulmonary vascular diseases. The results of principal component analysis highlight the value of this comprehensive approach. However, given the study's monocentric nature, the omission of PH Groups 4 and 5, and the lack of a healthy control cohort, larger-scale validation studies will be needed to confirm these findings.

articles.title: hBM-MSC-Derived EVs Improved Pulmonary Vascular Remodeling and Right Ventricle Function in a Mouse Pulmonary Hypertension Model

abstract.text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is characterized by elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP), pulmonary vascular remodeling, and right ventricle (RV) hypertrophy and failure. PH is a rare disease, with significant morbidity and limited therapeutic options. Human Mesenchymal Stem-cell derived (hMSC) extracellular vesicles (EVs) have shown potential in improving pulmonary artery flow and RV function. The aim of this study was to evaluate the therapeutic effects of hMSC-EVs in a mouse model of monocrotaline (MCT)-induced PH. MCT + EVs animals compared to MCT + vehicle alone demonstrated improvement in RV function with an increase in Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion by 37.1 ± 2.6% (p = 0.0011) and reduction in RV hypertrophy by 18.6 ± 7.6% (p = 0.0218) using Fulton's index. Pulmonary artery flow, evaluated by echocardiography of pulmonary artery acceleration time, was improved with EV treatment by 18.5 ± 1.3% (p = 0.0419). Histological studies demonstrated a corresponding reduction in pulmonary arteriolar muscularization by 41.2 ± 18.5% (p = 0.0004). Western blot analysis of MCT + EVs versus MCT + vehicle demonstrated modulations in proteins related to metabolism and cellular energetics in lungs and to calcium sequestration in RV. Proteomic analysis of circulating EVs from MCT + EVs versus MCT + vehicle groups revealed upregulation of proteasome and autophagy pathways in MCT + vehicle, which were attenuated by hMSC-EV. These results support a promising role for EVs in improving pulmonary vascular remodeling and RV function in PH by modulating signaling pathways involved in proteasome, autophagy, cellular energetic and metabolism.

articles.title: Left ventricular assist device implantation in a 'turtle-shell' sclerotic left ventricular apex: a case report of landing-zone selection and tailored fixation strategy

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation usually requires a compliant and structurally suitable left ventricular apex for coring, sewing-ring fixation, and inflow cannula alignment. Severe apical sclerosis may eliminate the conventional implantable apex.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 73-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and refractory advanced heart failure underwent Corheart-6 LVAD implantation. Preoperative imaging showed severe ventricular dilatation, biventricular dysfunction, functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and a markedly abnormal apical segment with thinning, akinesia, outward bulging, and mural mass formation. Intraoperatively, dense apical adhesions and a rigid 3- to 4-cm 'turtle-shell-like' sclerotic region were encountered. After limited dissection and repair of a localized rupture, the conventional apical target was considered unsuitable for safe coring and sewing-ring fixation. To preserve an acceptable inflow axis while avoiding major coronary structures, an adjacent viable myocardial landing zone at approximately the 5-o'clock position was selected. Circumferential pledgeted 3-0 Prolene sutures were used for reinforced sewing-ring fixation. Because the intracavitary pathway remained restrictive, limited assessment and targeted trimming of interfering secondary chordal tissue were performed only as needed to accommodate the inflow cannula. No obvious papillary muscle or major trabecular structure was resected. Implantation was completed with satisfactory haemostasis. The patient was discharged on postoperative Day 17 and remained clinically stable with normal daily activities at the 24-month follow-up.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In severe apical sclerosis, LVAD implantation should prioritize optimal inflow cannula position and feasible inflow-axis alignment. Landing-zone selection, reinforced fixation, and limited intracavitary modification are enabling manoeuvres to achieve an unobstructed inflow pathway.

articles.conclusion: In severe apical sclerosis, LVAD implantation should prioritize optimal inflow cannula position and feasible inflow-axis alignment. Landing-zone selection, reinforced fixation, and limited intracavitary modification are enabling manoeuvres to achieve an unobstructed inflow pathway.

Early outcomes of tricuspid valve replacement in patients with tricuspid regurgitation: the Trisol Early Feasibility Study
authors: on behalf of the Trisol investigators
articles.journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) could lead to a paradigm shift in treating tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and improving patient quality of life.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: We aimed to report the 30-day outcomes of the Trisol Early Feasibility Study (EFS).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The Trisol EFS was a single-arm, multicentre study that enrolled patients with symptomatic ≥severe TR despite optimal medical therapy to undergo TTVR with the Trisol system via transjugular access. The primary safety endpoint was the rate of device-related serious adverse events, including death, myocardial infarction, disabling stroke, life-threatening bleeding, renal failure requiring dialysis, and the need for surgery. The primary performance endpoints included technical and procedural success, while secondary endpoints included echocardiographic as well as functional and quality-of-life measures.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 19 patients, who were treated with a latest-generation Trisol 12-anchor valve, were included from August 2023 to September 2025. The mean age was 75.8 years (range 62 to 91), 78.9% were female, and 78.9% were in New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III or IV. TR was reduced to mild or less in 87.5% of the subjects and moderate or less in 100% of the subjects. The 30-day composite major adverse event rate was 10.5% (2/19) due to one cardiovascular death and one pacemaker implantation. No other complications were observed. NYHA Class significantly improved to Class I/II (87.5%), and the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score improved by a mean of 13.6±34.6 points.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this early clinical experience, the Trisol TTVR system demonstrated technical feasibility, overall safety, significant TR reduction, and the ability to improve quality of life and functional status in TR patients.

articles.conclusion: In this early clinical experience, the Trisol TTVR system demonstrated technical feasibility, overall safety, significant TR reduction, and the ability to improve quality of life and functional status in TR patients.

articles.title: Transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement after failed edge-to-edge repair
articles.journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Residual or recurrent tricuspid regurgitation (TR) after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is a growing concern in clinical practice and is associated with inferior outcomes.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: We sought to evaluate the early experience of transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) in patients with failed TEER.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study included patients undergoing TTVR for recurrent or residual severe TR after TEER. Clinical, echocardiographic, and computed tomography findings were evaluated. The primary outcome was clinical success at 30 days after TTVR.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 28 patients included (age 78.5±6.3 years, 61% female), 20 (72%) had residual TR and 8 (28%) had recurrent TR diagnosed within a median of 182 days after TEER. Patients were severely symptomatic (New York Heart Association [NYHA] III/IV in 97%), and 64% had massive/torrential TR. In 6 patients (21%), a commissural TEER device was evident, enabling direct TTVR (neocommissure strategy). Engagement of TEER devices with single leaflet device attachment during TTVR was carried out in 12 patients (43%), and electrosurgical laceration and stabilisation to facilitate TTVR in 10 patients (36%). Clinical success at 30 days was 93%. NYHA Functional Class improved in 93% of patients, with 85% being in NYHA I/II at 1 month after TTVR. Two patients died from non-cardiac reasons, and during a median follow-up of 69 days, 4 patients suffered a heart failure hospitalisation despite procedural success.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this small patient cohort, three different TTVR strategies after failed TEER resulted in significant clinical success at 30 days and led to substantial symptom relief during short-term follow-up.

articles.conclusion: In this small patient cohort, three different TTVR strategies after failed TEER resulted in significant clinical success at 30 days and led to substantial symptom relief during short-term follow-up.

articles.title: Peripheral Artery Disease in Acute Care Settings: Diagnosis and Management of Common Presentations and Emergencies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
authors: American Heart Association Acute Cardiac Care and General Cardiology Science Committee of the Council on Clinical Cardiology; Council on Cardiovascular and Stroke Nursing; Council on Cardiovascular Radiology and Intervention; Council on Lifelong Congenital Heart Disease and Heart Health in the Young; Council on Peripheral Vascular Disease; and Council on Quality of Care and Outcomes Research

abstract.text: People with peripheral artery disease (PAD) are often misdiagnosed or diagnosed late and, even after diagnosis, are undertreated with both pharmacologic and invasive therapies. The disease is associated with an increased risk of mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, other vascular disease, limb loss, and reduced quality of life. Although the risks and long-term management of PAD are well documented, these risks are acutely magnified when PAD exists as a comorbidity in patients hospitalized for other cardiovascular or medical conditions. Procedures requiring vascular access for the treatment of acute myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock, or valvular heart disease, as well as procedures for the treatment of the patient's underlying PAD, require special consideration in patients with PAD. Familiarity with the use and placement of mechanical circulatory support in patients with PAD, as well as the management of recent endovascular or surgical vascular interventions, is essential for providing appropriate care in the acute care setting.

articles.title: Zero-Contrast Transcatheter Aortic Valve-in-Valve Replacement Guided by Continuous Hemodynamic Monitoring
articles.journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstract.text: An 89-year-old man with structural deterioration of a surgical aortic bioprosthesis and renal dysfunction underwent zero-contrast transcatheter aortic valve-in-surgical valve (TAV-in-SAV) implantation. A SavvyWire provided continuous left ventricular pressure monitoring and rapid pacing during the procedure. After implantation of a 23-mm self-expanding valve, a residual transvalvular gradient was detected, prompting balloon postdilatation under rapid pacing. Repeat invasive hemodynamic assessment showed improvement, and echocardiography demonstrated a mean gradient of 12 mmHg. At 12 months, the patient was in New York Heart Association class I, with preserved renal function and a mean gradient of 8 mmHg. Continuous pressure monitoring may support intraprocedural assessment and guide valve optimization when contrast exposure is being avoided in patients with renal dysfunction.

articles.title: Sedentarism in the HFpEF Spectrum: Is Exercise the Remedy?

abstract.text: Sedentarism has a ubiquitous presence in contemporary society and is a growing issue across Asia. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has an increasing prevalence, and its pathophysiology and cardiac structural changes are closely linked to cardiac changes seen with sedentarism. Both sedentarism and HFpEF lead to increased mortality. Their systemic effects, underpinned by metabolic dysfunction driving chronic sterile inflammation, are felt in most organ systems. This review highlights the effects of sedentarism and HFpEF on organ systems and how exercise can remediate these changes. It will focus on the cardiovascular, skeletal, and respiratory systems, providing insight into molecular mechanisms. It will then review the benefits of exercise on each organ system and explore the utility of exercise as a treatment option for HFpEF, focusing on evidence from exercise trials in HFpEF. Finally, the review will propose an exercise rehabilitation regimen for the prevention and treatment of HFpEF.

articles.title: Orthostatic hypotension in continuous-flow LVADs: Baroreflex unloading, preload dependence, and a phenotype-specific framework

abstract.text: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is an underrecognized consequence of continuous-flow left ventricular assist device (CF-LVAD) therapy, affecting 12-30% of patients. Reduced arterial pulsatility during CF support creates a distinct autonomic environment characterized by impaired baroreceptor stimulation, defective sympathetic vasoconstriction, exaggerated venous pooling, and extreme preload dependence. Traditional blood pressure assessments often fail to identify OH in this population, and resting hemodynamics rarely reveal the underlying mechanism. In this perspective piece, we propose a two-phenotype, physiology-based framework for OH specific to CF-LVAD patients. We synthesize current knowledge of baroreflex biology, vascular capacitance, and pump dynamics to describe how reduced pulsatility disrupts cardiovascular responses to upright posture. Within this framework, we define two dominant mechanistic phenotypes: (1) autonomic dysfunction-predominant failure, where impaired reflexes drive orthostatic venous pooling and LV underfilling, and (2) right ventricular (RV) failure-limited forward flow, where RV dysfunction constrains preload delivery to the pump despite preserved autonomic tone. We outline how integrating autonomic data with LVAD hemodynamics and posture-linked imaging-specifically dynamic changes in venous capacitance, inferior vena cava behavior, left ventricular end-diastolic dimension, and pump performance-forms a coherent diagnostic and management pathway. This physiology-first approach allows clinicians to distinguish between preload failure and RV-limited flow at the bedside and tailor therapy accordingly. A mechanistic understanding of OH in CF-LVAD patients is essential for accurate diagnosis, preventing suction events, optimizing device settings, and reducing morbidity through targeted, mechanism-specific management.

articles.title: Long-Term Milrinone as a Bridge to Recovery in Fontan-Associated Protein-Losing Enteropathy

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) occurs in 5% to 18% of post-Fontan palliation patients with a historical mortality rate of 50%. Treatment of PLE continues to be challenging because of limited understanding of its pathophysiology.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 14-year-old boy with double outlet right ventricle and left ventricular hypoplasia with an extracardiac Fontan developed refractory PLE. He was started on long-term, outpatient milrinone at 0.5 μg/kg/min. Over 15 months, ventricular function improved and PLE resolved. Recovery was sustained 8 months after milrinone discontinuation.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Milrinone's augmentation of cardiac output and reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance may directly address PLE physiology. Long-term milrinone therapy has primarily been studied as a bridge to transplant. Notably, this case highlights milrinone's use as a bridge to recovery. The 15-month duration of milrinone was safe without adverse outcomes.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: Long-term outpatient milrinone therapy may serve as a bridge to recovery in patients with refractory Fontan-associated PLE.

articles.title: Right Ventricular Cardiomyocyte Dysfunction and Arrhythmogenesis in a Bleomycin-induced Mouse Model of Group 3 Pulmonary Hypertension
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
articles.journal_abbrev: Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol
articles.ta: Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol

abstract.text: Group 3 pulmonary hypertension (PH) occurs when lung diseases induce hypoxic vasoconstriction and pulmonary vascular remodeling. The increase in pulmonary vascular resistance elevates right ventricular (RV) afterload leading to progressive ventricular dysfunction. The mechanisms underlying cardiomyocyte dysfunction in Group 3 PH remain poorly characterized, despite RV pathology representing a critical component of disease progression. Using a mouse model of intratracheal bleomycin-induced PH, we tested the hypothesis that RV function and cardiomyocyte excitation-contraction coupling (ECC) are impaired in PH. Male and female mice were administered intratracheal saline (Sham) or bleomycin to induce PH and assess for sex differences across cardiac parameters. Langendorff-perfused working heart preparations revealed that PH mice display greater RV pressure development, elevated end diastolic pressure, and more spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias versus Sham. Structurally, hearts of PH mice exhibited increased RV hypertrophy and fibrosis versus Sham, with the hypertrophic response more pronounced in males versus females. To assess Ca2+ dynamics and cellular contractile function, enzymatically isolated cardiomyocytes were subjected to electrical field stimulation (0.5-4 Hz, fura-2 dye). RV cardiomyocyte ECC was impaired in PH versus Sham mice, including elevated diastolic Ca2+ and shorter diastolic sarcomere lengths, depressed Ca2+ transient and sarcomere contraction amplitudes, and slower Ca2+ decay rates with slower sarcomere relaxation. Left ventricular (LV) cardiomyocytes did not display these changes. Taken together, these data indicate impairment in RV ECC in the bleomycin-induced PH model, highlighting multiple Ca2+ handling abnormalities that may contribute to the RV dysfunction and arrhythmogenesis observed clinically in PH.

articles.title: Evaluating the Feasibility and Clinical Utility of Pre-Transplant Pharmacogenomic Testing in Adult Heart Transplant Recipients - A Pilot Study
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pharmacogenomic (PGx) testing identifies genetic variations that influence individual responses to medications. These genetically determined differences in drug metabolism necessitate personalized medication selection and dosage adjustments. Adult heart transplant recipients frequently receive multiple high-risk medications. Actionable findings from a priori screening of established PGx variants can optimize medication decisions, minimize toxicity, and reduce suboptimal therapeutic responses.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-center pilot study retrospectively assessed the feasibility of implementing CLIA-certified PGx testing, including 36 pharmacogenes in 79 adult heart transplant recipients. Patient phenotypes were interpreted as per the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) guidelines. Actionable gene-drug interactions and dosage recommendations were summarized for each patient by extracting clinical phenotypes, medication history, and PGx-guided prescription recommendations from the electronic health record (EHR).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The study identified clinically relevant gene-drug interactions including CYP3A5-tacrolimus, CYP2C19-voriconazole, and SLCO1B1-statin metabolism. 57% of the recipients were poor metabolizers/non-expressers of CYP3A5, while 43% were intermediate and extensive metabolizers/expressers. CYP3A5 expressers had higher tacrolimus dose requirements and modestly longer time to therapeutic trough concentrations compared with non-expressers. Genotype-guided changes to tacrolimus doses were made for 23 individuals. CYP2C19 phenotypes affecting voriconazole intake and SLCO1B1 phenotypes affecting statin dosing were also identified, with recommended dosage changes in 11 and 8 patients, respectively.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Pre-transplant PGx screening revealed a substantial burden of actionable drug-gene findings relevant to heart transplant pharmacotherapy. These preliminary results support the feasibility of pre-transplant PGx testing and may help inform larger studies aimed at PGx-guided care in transplantation.

articles.conclusion: Pre-transplant PGx screening revealed a substantial burden of actionable drug-gene findings relevant to heart transplant pharmacotherapy. These preliminary results support the feasibility of pre-transplant PGx testing and may help inform larger studies aimed at PGx-guided care in transplantation.

articles.title: Interdisciplinary Collaboration as Key Factor for the Optimization of Advanced Heart Failure Treatment

abstract.text: Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health problem, with outcomes in advanced stages continuing to be poor despite the development of medical therapy and interventional strategies. This report proposes the concept of Interdisciplinary Heart Failure Collaboration (IHFC), a structured framework designed to optimize patient outcomes through coordinated, cross-sectoral care, focusing on the management of advanced HF. The IHFC integrates a broad spectrum of healthcare professionals-including cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, nurses, anesthesiologists, intensivists, psychologists, ventricular assist device (VAD) coordinators, and many others-to provide optimal care from outpatient diagnosis to post-discharge long-term management. The model consists of three core management phases: 1) pre-hospital management, which includes outpatient clinic visits, accurate diagnosis and timely referral; 2) intra-hospital management, comprising interventional and surgical treatment including durable VAD implantation and heart transplantation; 3) post-discharge management; post-interventional and post-operative care, rehabilitation and long-term follow-up, patient education and support for self-care. In addition, this report discusses current challenges in implementation, including the need for standardized protocols and effective communication among team members. Rather than replacing existing HF care systems, the IHFC provides a practical framework for integrating established multidisciplinary principles across the entire clinical trajectory of advanced HF and may be adapted to different healthcare settings.

articles.title: Pulmonary Artery Dissection in Unrepaired Patent Ductus Arteriosus: Hemodynamic-Guided Ductal Closure

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pulmonary artery (PA) dissection is a rare and potentially fatal complication, usually associated with severe pulmonary hypertension, PA aneurysms, or congenital heart disease. Evidence regarding management remains limited.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 30-year-old man with unrepaired patent ductus arteriosus presented with acute chest pain and was diagnosed with PA dissection, giant PA aneurysm, severe pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension. He underwent urgent surgical repair, pulmonary valve replacement, and PA reconstruction. Given uncertain operability, transient intraoperative ductal reopening produced acute hemodynamic deterioration and right ventricular dysfunction, whereas occlusion improved pulmonary hemodynamics, supporting definitive closure.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: PA dissection associated with patent ductus arteriosus is exceptionally uncommon and presents complex management challenges. This case illustrates the value of intraoperative hemodynamic assessment when conventional operability evaluation is not feasible.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: Intraoperative hemodynamic testing may help guide ductal closure in selected high-risk patients with uncertain operability.

articles.title: Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction in Low-Income Settings: Performance and Challenges of Screening Scores in a Population-Based Cohort in Haiti
articles.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is rapidly increasing in low- and middle-income countries, however detection remains challenging. We assessed 2 screening scores developed in high-income settings, H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF, against physician-adjudicated HFpEF in a population-based cohort from Haiti.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The primary outcome was prevalent HFpEF defined by (1) physician adjudication, (2) H2FpEF score, (3) HFA-PEFF score. The cross-sectional cohort comprised 3003 adults from the Haiti Cardiovascular Disease Cohort, with sociodemographic, clinical, electrocardiography, echocardiography and BNP data available. We compared physician-adjudicated HFpEF participants to those screening positive (intermediate-high H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF scores) using interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha). Diagnostic performance of H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF against physician adjudication, used as a pragmatic reference standard appropriate for Haiti and similar settings, was calculated via sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Age-adjusted HFpEF prevalence was 9.5% (95% CI: 8.3-11.0) by physician adjudication, 10.2% (95% CI: 9.0-11.7) by H2FPEF, and 8.6% (95% CI: 7.5-10.0) by HFA-PEFF. Adjudicated HFpEF participants were young (median age 57), had high prevalence of hypertension (70%), obesity (33%), and no atrial fibrillation. Agreement between all 3 scores was moderate-substantial (alpha 0.57, 95% CI: 0.55-0.59), with the highest pair-wise agreement between physician adjudication and HFA-PEFF (kappa 0.62, 95% CI: 0.57-0.67). HFA-PEFF had higher sensitivity and similar specificity relative to H2FPEF.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this Haitian cohort, prevalent HFpEF occurred in relatively young participants with high hypertension and obesity rates and negligible atrial fibrillation. HFA-PEFF exhibited higher concordance and sensitivity than H2FPEF versus physician adjudication. Tailored, non-invasive HFpEF screening scores for low- and middle-income countries are needed to address this growing global epidemic.

articles.conclusion: In this Haitian cohort, prevalent HFpEF occurred in relatively young participants with high hypertension and obesity rates and negligible atrial fibrillation. HFA-PEFF exhibited higher concordance and sensitivity than H2FPEF versus physician adjudication. Tailored, non-invasive HFpEF screening scores for low- and middle-income countries are needed to address this growing global epidemic.

articles.title: Myocardial Hmgcs2-Driven Ketogenesis Promotes Atrial Fibrillation in Diabetes

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Type 2 diabetes (T2DM) increases the risk of atrial fibrillation (AF). Elevated circulating ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate [β-OHB]) in T2DM are considered hepatic in origin and benefit the heart via energy provision. Although we found ketogenesis enzyme Hmgcs2 (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase 2) upregulated in both atrial and ventricular tissues of T2DM mice, alongside increased cardiac and circulating β-OHB. Whether enhanced Hmgcs2 is related to AF, ketogenesis-dependent or independent, remained unclear.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: T2DM mice were induced by high-fat diet and followed by streptozocin injection. Cardiac-specific Hmgcs2 overexpression and cardiomyocyte-specific Hmgcs2 knockout were conducted in T2DM mice. Cardiac function and left atrial diameter were evaluated using echocardiography, and cardiac electrophysiology was examined through electrical mapping. Programmed electrical stimulation was delivered to induce AF. Blood metabolomics from the coronary sinus and left atria of patients with or without T2DM were analyzed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The heart functioned as a primary ketogenic organ in T2DM mice via upregulating Hmgcs2, surpassing the liver. Hmgcs2-mediated shunting of fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA into ketogenesis depleted myocardial energy reserves, exacerbated oxidative stress, and caused mitochondrial injury, ultimately increasing AF inducibility and diastolic dysfunction. In addition, cardiac-derived β-hydroxybutyrate released into circulation prolonged action potential duration in atrial cardiomyocytes. Mechanistically, Hmgcs2-mediated cytosolic β-hydroxybutyrylation targeted Oxct1 (3-oxoacid CoA-transferase 1) for degradation, blocking cardiac ketolysis. Blood metabolomics from the coronary sinus and left atria confirmed active cardiac ketogenesis in patients with T2DM and heart-derived ketone release into systemic circulation. Venous plasma β-OHB levels positively correlated with atrial low-voltage burden and postablation AF recurrence. Cardiomyocyte-specific Hmgcs2 knockdown improved cardiac utilization of fatty acids, β-OHB, and glucose in T2DM mice by suppressing cardiac ketogenesis; this intervention, with reduced circulating β-OHB, attenuated diabetes-associated AF.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Cardiac Hmgcs2 represented a novel therapeutic target for diabetic AF and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

articles.conclusion: Cardiac Hmgcs2 represented a novel therapeutic target for diabetic AF and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

articles.title: Systematic Transesophageal Echocardiographic Identification of Tricuspid Valve Commissures and Subvalvular Apparatus

abstract.text: Transcatheter tricuspid valve (TV) intervention is rapidly evolving and several classes of therapeutic devices are currently in development. The anatomic knowledge of the TV is the cornerstone for transcatheter patient selection, and the successful implantation of the devices depends on imaging guidance. Anatomically, leaflets are separated by the commissures, which have peculiar findings: they are supported by fan-shaped chords and do not open directly into the annulus, but a few millimeters of the leaflet tissue remain, similar to small scallops. While a comprehensive echocardiographic assessment of TV has been extensively reported, few papers have focused on analyzing commissures and their impact on interventions. This paper aims to introduce a novel echocardiographic approach focusing on TV commissures, and provide a dedicated transesophageal imaging protocol and methodology for recognizing their anatomic landmarks. Multiple dedicated transesophageal views are comprehensively reported for each commissure, in order to ensure a guide for emerging transcatheter procedures.

articles.title: Ventricular Morphology and Atrioventricular Valve Regurgitation in Adults Post-Fontan: Associations With Exercise Hemodynamics

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Right ventricular (RV) dominance and atrioventricular valve regurgitation (AVVR) are associated with adverse outcomes post-Fontan palliation, but their underlying hemodynamic correlates, particularly during exercise, remain incompletely characterized.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this cross-sectional cohort, exercise hemodynamics by ventricular morphology and AVVR severity were assessed invasively (supine exercise catheterization) in 108 individuals and semi-invasively (semisupine exercise with echocardiography and peripheral venous pressure) in 108.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Age of the invasive cohort was 32.1 (25.6-37.2) years; 41 had RV dominance, 19 had moderate or severe AVVR, and 16 had both. Resting and peak mean pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary artery wedge pressure were similar across ventricular morphologies and AVVR severity. However, RV dominance was associated with lower systemic (systemic blood flow, 67% [22-93] versus 86% [63-105] predicted; P=0.006) and pulmonary (pulmonary blood flow, 57% [33-75] versus 72% [61-89] predicted; P<0.001) cardiac output responses to exercise and steeper Δpulmonary artery pressure/Δpulmonary blood flow, (4.3 [2.6-10.6] versus 3.0 [1.7-4.8] mm Hg/L per minute; P=0.004). Patients with moderate or severe AVVR showed a similar pattern, with lower systemic blood flow (64% [19-92] versus 77% [57-101], P=0.10) and pulmonary blood flow (57% [36-74] versus 70% [55-88] predicted, P=0.03) responses. Findings were replicated in the semi-invasive cohort, where RV dominance and moderate or severe AVVR were associated with lower peak systemic blood flow and higher Δperipheral venous pressure/Δ systemic blood flow, despite similar peak peripheral venous pressure.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Resting and exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, and peripheral venous pressure are unrelated to ventricular morphology and AVVR severity. Conversely, impaired flow augmentation and steeper pressure-flow relationships during exercise were associated with RV dominance and moderate or severe AVVR, emphasizing the role of dynamic provocation to unmask occult cardiovascular reserve limitations.

articles.conclusion: Resting and exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, and peripheral venous pressure are unrelated to ventricular morphology and AVVR severity. Conversely, impaired flow augmentation and steeper pressure-flow relationships during exercise were associated with RV dominance and moderate or severe AVVR, emphasizing the role of dynamic provocation to unmask occult cardiovascular reserve limitations.

articles.title: Rapid-Onset Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia During Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Causing Cardiogenic Shock Due to Thrombotic Coronary Occlusions

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is one of the most common but potentially fatal immune-mediated adverse drug reactions and may develop with a rapid onset in patients re-exposed to heparin within 90 days of prior heparin administration.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A patient with chronic coronary syndrome developed recurrent thrombotic coronary occlusions during percutaneous coronary intervention because of rapid-onset HIT, resulting in in-hospital cardiac arrest complicated by cardiogenic shock requiring mechanical circulatory support. Intravenous immunoglobulin was administered as rescue therapy.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Unexplained and recurrent periprocedural coronary thrombosis during invasive coronary angiography should prompt consideration of HIT as a differential diagnosis.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Periprocedural coronary thrombosis during percutaneous coronary intervention because of rapid-onset HIT is a rare and potentially life-threatening condition that may occur in patients re-exposed to heparin following recent heparin administration. Intravenous immunoglobulin G should be considered in severe refractory HIT.

articles.title: Sex differences in temporary mechanical circulatory support, vascular complications, and mortality in acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock: a contemporary national analysis, 2016 to 2023

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: Women with acute myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) have historically received mechanical circulatory support (MCS) less often than men and have had higher mortality. Whether these differences persist in the contemporary era, and how vascular and access complications differ by sex across device types, is uncertain.

abstract.label: METHODS AND RESULTS
abstract.text: Using the National Inpatient Sample (2016 to 2023), we identified 66 381 admissions (331 905 weighted) with acute myocardial infarction and a secondary diagnosis of cardiogenic shock, of whom 34.2% were women. MCS was classified as intra-aortic balloon pump, percutaneous left ventricular assist device, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Associations with female sex were estimated using survey-weighted logistic regression; race and hospital region, unavailable in 2023, were adjusted in a 2016 to 2022 sensitivity analysis. After adjustment, women were less likely than men to receive any MCS [odds ratio (OR) 0.77, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.80] and each device. Women had higher in-hospital mortality overall (OR 1.17, 1.13 to 1.22) and among recipients (OR 1.18, 1.11 to 1.26), without significant variation by device (interaction P = 0.74). Women had more acute limb ischaemia (OR 1.76) and blood transfusion (OR 1.27), consistently across device types. In sequential models further adjusted for device and coded complications, the mortality difference persisted (OR 1.22).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In contemporary practice, women with AMI-CS received less MCS and had higher mortality and more access-site complications than men. The mortality difference persisted after adjustment and should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding by unmeasured shock severity cannot be excluded.

articles.conclusion: In contemporary practice, women with AMI-CS received less MCS and had higher mortality and more access-site complications than men. The mortality difference persisted after adjustment and should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding by unmeasured shock severity cannot be excluded.

articles.title: Design and rationale of MIRACLE, a prospective multicenter cohort study with integrated biobanking in cardiogenic shock

abstract.label: RATIONALE
abstract.text: Cardiogenic shock carries high mortality, yet most evidence comes from patients with shock related to acute myocardial infarction. Cohorts that combine serial staging, repeated biobanking, and structured assessment of survivors across severity stages and etiologies are scarce.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: MIRACLE (multimodal phenotyping in patients referred with acute cardiac failure) aims at multimodal phenotyping and risk stratification of patients with cardiogenic shock across etiologies. The primary endpoint is all-cause mortality at 30 days.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Prospective, observational, multicenter cohort study with an embedded biobank. Adults with Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) stage B preshock or stage C to E shock of any etiology are enrolled in intensive and intermediate care units. Patients with a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction without shock are enrolled as controls (SCAI A) for shock related to myocardial infarction. SCAI stages are reassessed during the first 24 hours after admission to intensive care and at study visits on days 1, 3, and 5 and at discharge from intensive care, each with biobanking. Follow-up extends to 12 months and includes a visit at 6 months with repeat biobanking, exercise testing, cognitive assessment, and patient-reported outcomes.

abstract.label: SITES
abstract.text: Four centers in Germany.

abstract.label: ESTIMATED ENROLLMENT
abstract.text: Approximately 600 patients, ≥ 500 day-1 samples.

abstract.label: ENROLLMENT DATES
abstract.text: August 2024 to the middle of 2027 (estimated).

abstract.label: CURRENT STATUS
abstract.text: As of 30 September 2026, 449 patients with shock or preshock and 22 controls had been enrolled. Blood samples on day 1 were obtained in 88% of eligible patients, and follow-up at 6 months was completed in 86% of eligible survivors, at the study site in 148 and by telephone in 62. Mortality at 30 days was 15% in SCAI stage B and 63% in stage E (overall 35%). Enrollment is limited to German academic centers, and very early deaths may have been missed.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07515508, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07515508.

articles.title: Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Mortality in Pediatric Medical Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)

abstract.text: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is increasingly used in pediatric refractory cardiac arrest. This study investigated the association between ECPR and mortality in pediatric patients receiving venoarterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) for medical indications. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients aged 28 days to <18 years who received VA-ECMO at a tertiary referral children's hospital between January 2010 and May 2025. The primary outcome was pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) mortality. Among 73 patients (non-ECPR, n = 58; ECPR, n = 15), ECPR was associated with increased mortality in unadjusted analysis (odds ratio [OR], 5.23; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.47-18.53; p = 0.010). After adjustment for pre-ECMO physiologic variables, the association between ECPR and mortality was no longer significant (adjusted OR, 1.74; 95% CI, 0.37-8.08; p = 0.483). Lower pre-ECMO arterial pH remained associated with higher mortality (adjusted OR, 1.87 per 0.1 decrease; 95% CI, 1.20-2.92; p = 0.006). In a sensitivity analysis, underlying cardiac disease was associated with lower mortality than noncardiac disease (adjusted OR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.07-0.79; p = 0.020). These findings highlight the associations of pre-ECMO physiologic status and underlying disease category with PICU mortality.

articles.title: Prognostic Value of Left Ventricular Kinetic Energy Assessed by 4D Flow CMR in Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Alterations in left ventricular intracavitary hemodynamics can occur early in the course of nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). However, the association between 4-dimensional (4D) flow cardiac magnetic resonance parameters and adverse outcomes in patients with DCM remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate whether 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance parameters can predict adverse outcomes in patients with DCM.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this multicenter prospective cohort study, 675 adult patients with DCM (mean age, 56 years; 399 men) from 3 medical centers and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance. Left ventricular flow components and kinetic energy parameters were quantified. The primary end point was a composite of heart failure events, including heart failure-related death, unplanned heart failure hospitalization, or cardiac transplantation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: During a median follow-up of 42 months, 58 patients (8.6%) experienced the primary end point. Compared with controls, patients with DCM exhibited reduced peak systolic kinetic energy normalized to EDV (KEiEDV) and peak E-wave KEiEDV; these differences were more pronounced in those who developed the primary end point. In univariable Cox regression, direct flow, residual volume, peak systolic KEiEDV, and peak E-wave KEiEDV were significant predictors of the primary end point (all P<0.05). After adjustment for left ventricular ejection fraction, NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), extracellular volume fraction, extent of late gadolinium enhancement, peak systolic KEiEDV (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.39 [95% CI, 0.28-0.53]), and peak E-wave KEiEDV (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.26-0.48]) remained independently associated with the primary end point (both P<0.001). Furthermore, these 2 kinetic energy parameters provided incremental prognostic value beyond clinical markers and conventional imaging markers for predicting the primary end point.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In patients with DCM, decreased peak systolic KEiEDV and peak E-wave KEiEDV, as measured by 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance, are independently associated with poor prognosis and provide incremental prognostic value for risk stratification beyond clinical and conventional imaging markers.

abstract.label: REGISTRATION
abstract.text: URL:https://clinicaltrials.gov/; Unique Identifier: NCT07527715.

articles.conclusion: In patients with DCM, decreased peak systolic KEiEDV and peak E-wave KEiEDV, as measured by 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance, are independently associated with poor prognosis and provide incremental prognostic value for risk stratification beyond clinical and conventional imaging markers.

articles.title: Echocardiographic Left Atrial Stiffness Index as a Predictor of All-Cause Mortality in Non-Ischemic Dilated Cardiomyopathy
articles.journal: Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography : official publication of the American Society of Echocardiography

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: Reliable predictors of adverse outcomes in non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (NIDCM) remain limited. We aimed to evaluate the association between the left atrial stiffness index (LASI) and all-cause mortality in patients with NIDCM and to assess its prognostic value beyond established left atrial and diastolic markers.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Retrospective analysis of a prospectively recruited cohort of patients diagnosed with NIDCM between 2018 and 2022. All patients underwent comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography at the time of diagnosis. Left atrial (LA) strain was measured retrospectively from stored baseline echocardiograms using two-dimensional speckle-tracking analysis, and LASI was calculated as the ratio of E/e' to LA reservoir strain. Multivariable analyses were performed to identify variables independently associated with all-cause mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 200 patients (mean age 61.7 years; 40% women), 33 (16.5%) died over a median follow-up of 43.8 months. In multivariable Cox regression analysis, variables independently associated with all-cause mortality were LASI (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.92, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.33-2.77), age (HR 1.05, 95% CI 1.02-1.08) and right ventricular-pulmonary artery (RV-PA) coupling index (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.07-0.89); the model showed good discrimination (optimism-corrected C-index 0.766). LASI remained independently associated with mortality when modeled together with left atrial volume index (LAVi) and with E/e'.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In NIDCM, LASI provides prognostic information for all-cause mortality beyond other morphological and functional LA markers. Given the single-center design and the limited number of events, these findings warrant external validation.

articles.conclusion: In NIDCM, LASI provides prognostic information for all-cause mortality beyond other morphological and functional LA markers. Given the single-center design and the limited number of events, these findings warrant external validation.

articles.title: Pulmonary Artery Pressures Predict Heart Failure Events Following Heart Failure and Non-Heart Failure Events

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: It is uncertain whether pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) within the first week after either hospitalization for a non-heart failure event (HFE) or hospitalization or urgent visit for a HFE predicts the risk of recurring events.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study aims to determine if PAP following a non-HFE or HFE predicts subsequent events within 90 days.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The authors examined non-HFE and HFE in patients with heart failure (HF) treated with remote hemodynamic-guided management using a wireless PAP sensor in the GUIDE-HF study. They compared PAP trends before and after a non-HFE or HFE and stratified the admitting and discharge PAP during the index event into groups with a subsequent HFE, non-HFE, or no further events within 90 days.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Following index non-HFE (615 events, n = 425), post-discharge diastolic PAP was significantly higher in patients with a subsequent HFE (23.3 ± 7.9 mm Hg) (n = 97) vs patients with a subsequent non-HFE (20.4 ± 7.3 mm Hg; P = 0.0046) (n = 189) or no further events (20.9 ± 7.4 mm Hg; P = 0.015) (n = 329). Following index HFE (539 events, n = 358), post-discharge diastolic PAP was numerically higher in patients with a subsequent HFE (23.9 ± 6.9 mm Hg) (n = 199) than in patients with a subsequent non-HFE (22.0 ± 7.1 mm Hg; P = 0.078 (n = 102) and in those with no further events (22.0 ± 7.6 mm Hg; P = 0.021) (n = 238). Similar trends were observed for HF with reduced ejection fraction and HF with preserved ejection fraction subgroups and with systolic and mean PAP.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Persistently elevated PAP early after discharge following either an index non-HFE or an HFE is associated with the risk of a subsequent HFE. (Hemodynamic-GUIDEd Management of Heart Failure [GUIDE-HF]; NCT03387813).

articles.conclusion: Persistently elevated PAP early after discharge following either an index non-HFE or an HFE is associated with the risk of a subsequent HFE. (Hemodynamic-GUIDEd Management of Heart Failure [GUIDE-HF]; NCT03387813).

articles.title: Right ventricular apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric left ventricular septal involvement decades after heart transplant: a case report

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Long-term heart transplant (HT) survivors are an expanding population at risk for late, underrecognized complications. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy developing in the cardiac allograft is exceptionally rare, and right ventricular involvement complicates risk stratification for sudden cardiac death.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 30-year-old woman who underwent heart transplantation at 5 weeks for hypoplastic left heart syndrome was found to have right ventricular apical hypertrophy on surveillance transthoracic echocardiography. Sixteen months later, echocardiography demonstrated worsening right ventricular apical hypertrophy and new asymmetric left ventricular septal hypertrophy, without outflow tract obstruction. Cardiac magnetic resonance confirmed right ventricular apical hypertrophy (22 mm) extending into asymmetric septal hypertrophy (15 mm) with patchy late gadolinium enhancement involving approximately 30% of the myocardial mass, consistent with right ventricular apical variant hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric left ventricular septal involvement. She remained asymptomatic. Given the extensive late gadolinium enhancement burden, a subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was placed for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death. She remains asymptomatic 16 months later with no device-detected arrhythmias.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: To our knowledge, this is the first report of right ventricular apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular septal involvement in a HT recipient. Cardiac magnetic resonance characterized structurally significant but clinically silent disease, supporting a lower threshold for its use when surveillance echocardiography is abnormal after transplantation. Extensive late gadolinium enhancement in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy involving the right ventricle may warrant greater weight in sudden cardiac death risk stratification than current guidelines specify.

articles.title: Early Implementation of Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy and Outcomes in Cardiogenic Shock Supported by Micro-Axial Flow Pumps

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The role of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in patients with cardiogenic shock (CS) supported by mechanical circulatory support remains poorly defined. The feasibility and potential benefits of early GDMT initiation during Impella support are uncertain.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We analyzed a multicenter prospective registry of consecutive patients with CS treated with Impella between 2020 and 2024. GDMT exposure was defined as the number of heart failure therapies administered at device explantation. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for clinical severity and early shock trajectory. Landmark analysis excluded patients dying within 5 days, while mixed-effects models accounted for center-level clustering.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 140 patients (mean age 61 years; 20% female), 40% received concomitant ECMO (ECPella). In-hospital mortality was 38%. At explantation, 43% received at least one GDMT agent. Greater GDMT exposure was independently associated with lower mortality (OR 0.28 per additional therapy; 95% CI 0.14-0.58; p<0.001). This association remained consistent in landmark analysis (adjusted OR 0.31; 95% CI 0.16-0.66; p<0.001) and after excluding patients with cardiac arrest (adjusted OR 0.48; 95% CI 0.23-0.88; p=0.002).
